prompt: In a closed model, what decides how many requests a second the test sends?
hint: Nobody writes the rate down in a closed model.

choices.text: A rate of requests a second written in the script
choices.why: That is the open model. A closed test states users and think time, and the rate comes out of them.

choices.text: Users, think time and response time
choices.why: Right. Each user sends one request per loop, and the loop lasts the response plus the think time.

choices.text: The length of the ramp-up
choices.why: The ramp decides how fast the users start, not how often each one sends once started.

choices.text: The number of processors on the generator
choices.why: A generator with spare processors still waits for each answer before the next request.

prompt: The server under a closed test slows from 20 ms to two seconds a request. What happens to the load the test offers?
hint: What is every virtual user doing while it waits?

choices.text: It stays the same, since the user count did not change
choices.why: The users are the same, and each one now sends far less often, because it waits for every answer.

choices.text: It rises, because the users retry the slow requests
choices.why: Nothing in a closed loop retries; it waits, then thinks, then sends the next one.

choices.text: It moves to an open model on its own
choices.why: The model is a property of the generator, and it does not change mid-run.

choices.text: It falls, as each user waits longer
choices.why: Right. The users slow down with the server, so the test asks for less exactly when the server struggles.

prompt: Which of these systems is modelled best by a closed workload?
hint: Does anybody new arrive while the system is slow?

choices.text: Eight workers draining a job queue
choices.why: Right. The population is fixed at eight, and none of them starts a job before finishing the last.

choices.text: The box office when a popular show goes on sale
choices.why: People at a sale arrive whether or not the server has answered the people before them.

choices.text: A news site in the minutes after a big headline
choices.why: Readers arriving from a headline do not wait for each other: an open arrival rate.

choices.text: A public API called by thousands of unrelated clients
choices.why: Unrelated clients arrive independently, which is the open model.

prompt: A closed test with too few users reports a public site as slow but error-free, while a real crowd brings it down. What went wrong in the test?

choices.text: The users thought for too long between requests
choices.why: Long think time lowers the rate, but the defect is that the rate fell further when the server slowed.

choices.text: The ramp-up was too slow to reach the load
choices.why: A slow ramp delays the load; it does not remove it once the users are running.

choices.text: The slowdown stopped the users sending the requests that would have exposed it
choices.why: Right. Generator and server coordinated without meaning to, and the missing requests were the slow ones.

choices.text: The site had a cache the crowd did not hit
choices.why: Possible on some site, and nothing in the description points to it; the model explains it on its own.

prompt: A hundred virtual users with no think time sent 140 requests a second to the box office. What did that run measure?
hint: How much would a hundred people reading each page for four seconds ask for?

choices.text: The load that a hundred real people would put on the server
choices.why: A hundred people thinking four seconds each ask for about 25 a second, not 140.

choices.text: How much the server could finish, whatever was asked
choices.why: Right. With no pause, every user resends the moment it is answered, so the server sets the rate.

choices.text: The arrival rate of the ten o'clock sale
choices.why: The sale is an arrival rate worked out from people and visits; this run has no people in it.

choices.text: The capacity of the load generator
choices.why: The generator kept a hundred requests in flight; it was waiting on the server, not the other way round.

prompt: A virtual user is paced at one iteration every 10 seconds, and an iteration's requests take 3 seconds. How many seconds does it sleep before the next iteration?
hint: Pacing is measured from start to start.

prompt: Why does a load test ramp its users up instead of starting them all at once?
hint: Two hundred users starting in the same instant send what?

choices.text: Because generators refuse to start many threads together
choices.why: A generator can start them together; it is the result that suffers.

choices.text: To make the test run for longer
choices.why: The length of the run is set separately; the ramp is measured apart from it.

choices.text: So the test does not open with a burst nobody asked for
choices.why: Right. A start in one instant is a spike, and it would describe itself instead of the load being tested.

choices.text: So the think time can be shorter
choices.why: Think time is a property of the users, and the ramp does not change it.

prompt: Think time is counted from the end of an answer; pacing is counted from the ___ of one iteration to the ___ of the next.
hint: Pacing does not care how long the answer took.

prompt: Requests arrive at a server at 50 a second and each spends 0.2 seconds inside it. On average, how many requests are inside at once?
Thirty virtual users think for 2.9 seconds each, and the server answers in 0.1 seconds. How many requests a second do they send?
hint: N = X × (R + Z), solved for X.

prompt: Little's law is written with means, in a course that warns against the mean. Why is the mean right here?
hint: What kind of statement is the law?

choices.text: Because percentiles are not defined for a queue
choices.why: Percentiles of time in a queue exist and are useful; they are just not what the law relates.

choices.text: Because the box office is too small to need a percentile
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; the law holds for any stable system.

choices.text: Because lesson 8 says the mean is right for throughput
choices.why: Lesson 8 is about reading response times; the reason here is the law's own.

choices.text: Because the law is an identity about totals
choices.why: Right. Totals divided by time give means, and the identity holds between those means exactly.

prompt: Five people for every one of the 300 seats arrive in the first minute, and each visit is five requests. How many requests a second does the site receive in that minute?
hint: People a second, times requests a person.

prompt: Why does the sale's split by operation matter more than its total of 100 requests a second?
hint: Are all five requests of a visit the same cost?

choices.text: The show page is the costly read and the booking takes a lock
choices.why: Right. 60 a second of the expensive read and 20 of the locked write are two different tests.

choices.text: Totals are not allowed in a requirement
choices.why: A total can go in a requirement; it just hides which operation will fail first.

choices.text: The list of shows is cached by the browser
choices.why: Nothing in the box office says so, and the list is the cheapest of the three anyway.

choices.text: Every operation needs its own load generator
choices.why: One generator can send all three; the split is about what each costs the server.

prompt: The model said 240 users thinking 4 s would send 60 requests a second, and the box office received 59.9. What else had to be true for the two to agree?
hint: Look at R in the output.

choices.text: That the ramp lasted exactly ten seconds
choices.why: The ramp only decides when measurement starts; any length would give the same steady rate.

choices.text: That the requests went to one show
choices.why: Any show page costs about the same; the agreement does not depend on which.

choices.text: That the server kept up, so R stayed small
choices.why: Right. At 18.2 ms the response time added almost nothing to the 4 s loop; a slow server would have cut the rate.

choices.text: That no other test was running on the machine at the time
choices.why: Other work makes the numbers noisier, and the arithmetic agreed with it present.

prompt: Put the steps from a crowd to a number of virtual users in order.
hint: The order of "The ten o'clock sale, as a number".
items: estimate how many people arrive, and when
divide by the time to get people a second
multiply by the requests each visit makes
multiply by response time plus think time

prompt: A test sized at 101 users and 2 s of think time, to offer 50 requests a second, reports 25 a second and no errors, with responses near 2 s. What does it tell you about the requirement of 50 a second?

choices.text: It was met, since no request failed
choices.why: No request failed because only 25 a second were sent; the requirement asks about 50.

choices.text: Nothing, since 50 a second was never offered
choices.why: Right. 101 / (2 + 2) is about 25. Run it as an arrival rate, or size it for the real R, to ask the question.

choices.text: That the server's capacity is 50 requests a second
choices.why: It answered 25 a second at about 2 s each; nothing here shows it carrying 50.

choices.text: That the think time should be raised to compensate
choices.why: Longer think time would send even less; the users were already the limit.

prompt: A closed test must offer 30 requests a second, with 5 seconds of think time and responses of 0.5 seconds. How many virtual users does it need?
Match each term to what it means.
hint: Two of them are about time between requests.

pairs.right: the pause from an answer to the next request
a fixed interval from one iteration's start to the next
the period over which the users are started
a loop that sends, waits, thinks and sends again
requests a second, whether or not earlier ones were answered

right_distractors: the time the server spends on one request
